The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface

📅 2026-09-09 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that that contract is officially changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that that contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a newly introduced generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our customers to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.

This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.

The ultimate goal of modern web design is no longer to build prettier buttons or flashy animations; it is to eliminate the interface entirely.

Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.

It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.

To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.

It has been revealed that consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:.

This is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.

According to recent reports, intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?

When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.

Industry observers note that this shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.

According to recent reports, traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.

According to recent reports, perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.

Recent findings suggest that for years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.

Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.

Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent owners or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.

Industry observers note that when you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:.

Sources indicate that an invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.

In a recent development, in traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store highlights the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.

In a recent development, as highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a newly introduced UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.

Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering users with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).

Intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.

In a recent development, while removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.

When a website makes decisions for you, it can promptly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.

Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).

In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the concern — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.

With an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so consumers can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.

As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.

Rather than designing static buttons and rigid forms, we need to learn to map and present dynamic, generative UI components that adapt on the fly to user intent.

By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.

According to recent reports, for decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.

The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,.

It has been revealed that we are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.

#45938. Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2561 w)
📖 Baca

Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK. After graduating from the University of London with a Masters Degree … More about Alex ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

And proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS tech giant, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

Companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

Most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

According to recent reports, so the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch users struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the tech giant’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of latest consumers’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

One warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

In a recent development, ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

Direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in new syncs and shared dashboards.

The line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.

Industry observers note that add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own.

It has been revealed that most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the new pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles.

After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing: run the old experience against the latest one on an even traffic split until the sample means something.

Onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of newly introduced trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established.

Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation.

According to recent reports, A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example.

The team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with.

Leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone.

It has been revealed that so what did Meridian actually earn? The tech giant sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in fresh ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000.

Set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force.

It has been revealed that three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts fresh ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was.

Recent findings suggest that what persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides.

Budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process, but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.”.

A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI. Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard. Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in newly introduced ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost.

Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid.

In a recent development, scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows.

Meridian could say that NPS among trial consumers on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one.

According to recent reports, brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare, and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers.

Whatever you collect, systematize the collecting. Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present.

UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to firm-wide objectives, so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation.

Industry observers note that nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for: the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment.

This topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX.

Industry observers note that A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact, which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit.

When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight people, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

Recent findings suggest that but now, Brinkmann indicates his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

In a recent development, long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Industry observers note that greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

According to recent reports, the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann indicates, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

Sources indicate that the rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann claims. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

Industry observers note that vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

According to recent reports, the most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann notes. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

It has been revealed that “He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”.

Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

Recent findings suggest that “It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann indicates. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

Industry observers note that they discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann claims. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

It has been revealed that none of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

Recent findings suggest that this portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann notes. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

According to recent reports, it is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.
  • It has been revealed that dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds.
  • The Zero-Day sci-fi corridor highlights an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

It has been revealed that dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

The Zero-Day sci-fi corridor highlights an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

That matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

In a recent development, you can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

#45935. Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

📅 2026-09-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”.

I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a latest feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

Kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

It has been revealed that the bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

Sources indicate that note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

Recent findings suggest that the viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

Industry observers note that I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”.

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:.

Recent findings suggest that this changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

See the Pen [Viewport vs Container [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73d-6f39-709f-8dae-037f6b588852) by Vayo.

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

Media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

Sources indicate that container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In a recent development, in other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

An element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

In a recent development, in case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

Sources indicate that I’m not hating on media queries. It’s that in this era of responsiveness and component re-use, layout logic is closer to the container than the viewport. When we think in terms of containers and components, we’re effectively relying on the content to determine layout, not the viewport.

Responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

This works until that same component is moved into a different context, like a sidebar, where the viewport is completely irrelevant. Now, because we tied the responsiveness to the wrong reference point, the scaled typography can get too significant or too small.

Container queries come with their very own units — cqi, cqw, cqb, among others — and we can take responsive components further by coupling those units with the CSS clamp() function, using it for fluid typography that scales with the component rather than the viewport:.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

With this in place, the entire code is self-contained to that element’s specific container.

It has been revealed that interestingly, container queries can, in a way, detect the state of a component’s internal layout. It’s not bulletproof, but it is also something media queries simply cannot do because they only observe the external browser window and are structurally blind to internal layout events like when, for example, flex items wrap onto a new line. Let’s poke at that.

Flexbox is superb at wrapping content (flex-wrap: wrap), allowing flex items to automatically wrap to latest lines when the flex container runs out of space to fit them in a single row. But CSS by itself can’t tell when that wrap happens. There isn’t something like a :wrapped pseudo-class or a media query like @media (flex-wrapped: true) that would get us there.

Industry observers note that media queries only observe the browser window, as they can’t see internal changes. That is pretty much what flex wrapping is: a width state change on the item itself.

Industry observers note that for example, if you have a horizontal menu that is lined up with flexbox and you want the items to restyle themselves only when wrapped, you’d be in JavaScript territory, using ResizeObserver to get that information. However, when we nest container queries inside flex items, we can come up with a workaround to get what we need without JavaScript, thanks to this technique I learned from Kevin Powell. The core idea is to allow a flex item to flex-grow: 1 when we query the container’s inline size.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

Industry observers note that this works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles.

See the Pen [Flex Wrap Detection Using Container Queries [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a752-150a-754e-a77a-07fe1b046658) by Vayo.

Container queries, like all things, come with some side effects or caveats you will want to watch for before reaching for them.

Container queries need something similar to a parent-child relationship to function as expected. Let’s say we have this markup:.

We can’t actually query the .card component to adjust the .card-content, like this:.

This doesn’t work because a container cannot query itself. In that last example, we’re querying a card container and then attempting to adjust that container’s display based on its size. It’s an infinite loop.

Instead, we need an additional wrapper that makes the .card a descendant of the container:.

From there, we can query the .cards container and adjust the .card layout accordingly:.

In media queries, this doesn’t matter as @media does not care which element you style inside the block; its only concern is the viewport, which is always available. So you can just slap a condition on any element and call it a day.

This happens when querying the container’s size (i.e., its block, or vertical, size) instead of its inline-size:.

Why? Because the browser calculates the container’s dimensions without looking at its children. If we don’t give the .hero-banner an explicit height (or min-height or aspect-ratio), the browser sets a height of 0px.

In a recent development, for that reason, it’s often better to query a container by its inline-size instead. That is, unless you genuinely need to query the container’s block size.

Media queries aren’t affected by this, as they treat height the same way they treat @media (min-height: ...) does, i.e., ask the viewport and move on.

Another container query limitation: we can’t query against a custom property value:.

Sources indicate that this is because custom properties depend on values that cascade down the DOM tree. There’s the possibility that a container query that relies on a custom property can change that same custom property. And it can quickly get complicated:.

In a recent development, I don’t think any project should wholesale use @container instead of @media. Media queries still play an key role in responsive layouts. It’s about understanding the separation of concerns.

Recent findings suggest that I tend to reach for container queries when a component is used in more than one layout context. For example, a .card element could live in a full-width grid or a narrower sidebar. If that’s the case, then we’ll want the component’s content to determine when it adjusts rather than a media query that looks at the outer viewport.

Similarly, I reach for media queries when a component solely exists at the page level. This would be something like a main navigation that always sits at the top of the page. It is directly influenced by the viewport’s size, meaning that the viewport is a reliable reference for when the navigation needs to adjust. Again, it’s all about “macro” layout versus “micro” layouts.

Here’s a diagram for how I reason about which type of query to use:.

Industry observers note that at the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “latest”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps.

What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years.
  • Sources indicate that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser.
  • “After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.

Sources indicate that heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.

“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller mentioned in a statement.

It has been revealed that “From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”.

Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”.

Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.

It has been revealed that the fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.

A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.

The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington said: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”.

He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”.

Sources indicate that exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.

It has been revealed that before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.

The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.

Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, remarked of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”.

A Practical Guide To Naming Things

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that naming is hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

The site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

Sources indicate that how would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, currently with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Recent findings suggest that of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

Recent findings suggest that what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

As Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

According to recent reports, how to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent manufacturer of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the latest system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

According to recent reports, it’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Sources indicate that good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

In a recent development, the map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

According to recent reports, the right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and people. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

So if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

Industry observers note that we hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

We love seeing what we all can do to make the web more accessible and usable. Photography by César Béjar.

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio remarked the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” noted the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”.

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio noted.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-proposal layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

Rosadoce’s distinct front elevation is formed from a series of staggered openings, described by the studio as evoking an “inverted stair”. This allows in light and ventilation while maintaining privacy.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”.

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

Photography by César Béjar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

“By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” says a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

Industry observers note that the calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

According to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

Meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, says in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

#45928. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2070 w)

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

In a recent development, sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

It has been revealed that the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses firm-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these latest systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

It has been revealed that I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

In a recent development, the main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

One strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more promptly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

According to recent reports, but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Sources indicate that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a new tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

According to recent reports, at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

Industry observers note that but formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff revealed their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made.

Sources indicate that many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a latest tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

Industry observers note that what they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

This time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Industry observers note that look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

In a recent development, staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

In a recent development, but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

Sources indicate that that said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

It has been revealed that today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Recent findings suggest that take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

In a recent development, unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are presently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

It has been revealed that and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Tech giant data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

The instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it indicates exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Sources indicate that look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Sources indicate that organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

Recent findings suggest that however, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out new technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.
